blindSummary:
This country is one of the most legally transformed in its region for trans visitors. The 2019 constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; a 2022 family code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — a July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. A state sex-education centre runs an official trans-care programme, and the capital has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: the country is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the era of military-run forced-labour camps for gay men in the late 1960s is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
blindOutOfScope: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travellers; legal-gender-recognition mechanics are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: Legal-information platform overview (May 2026): this country's transformation from one of the most repressive systems (military-run forced-labour camps for gay men, 1965-68, with 'curing' experiments) to one of the most progressive legal frameworks - the 2019 constitution bans SOGI discrimination, the 2022 family code legalised same-sex marriage and adoption, and trans people can change legal gender without surgery - but a meaningful gap remains between law and daily reality.
